Evaluations across 6 models and 20 GPU configurations demonstrate that Coral reduces serving costs by up to 2.79$\times$ compared to the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 2.39$\times$ higher goodput under scarce resource constraints.
author: Yixuan Mei, Zikun Li, Zixuan Chen, Shiqi Pan, Mengdi Wu, Xupeng Miao, Zhihao Jia, K. V. Rashmi

title: Diversity-Aware Active Learning Builds Materials Datasets for Current and Future Objectives
content:
arXiv:2605.05104v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Materials science data collection can be expensive, making dataset reuse and long-term utility important for future discovery. In practice, data collection often prioritizes properties of current interest while other properties are excluded from the acquisition process. This can produce datasets that are well suited for current objectives but lose information needed for properties of future interest. Here, we present how to construct datasets that remain informative for both. We develop and evaluate acquisition frameworks that combine predictive disagreement with diversity in material features, predicted outcomes, or both. We test these approaches across four DFT datasets and an experimental thermoelectric dataset. Diversity inclusion in dataset construction can reduce present and future objectives trade-off by preserving a broader range of materials and property behavior during acquisition. Across all datasets, the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II with disagreements and feature diversity (NSGA-II Dis. + diversity) framework developed in this work provides the most robust balance between current and future objectives. It maintains prediction performance above random sampling for current objectives while mitigating bias on excluded properties and, in many cases, improving their performance beyond random sampling. This diversity-aware acquisition framework provides a practical route to building materials datasets with unbiased quality entries and mitigating cold-start limitations in subsequent modeling and discovery campaigns.
author: Rafael Espinosa Casta\~neda, Ashley Dale, Hongchen Wang, Yonatan Kurniawan, Hao Wan, Runze Zhang, Adji Bousso Dieng, Kangming Li, Jason Hattrick-Simpers

title: Optimizing Social Utility in Sequential Experiments
content:
arXiv:2605.06520v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Regulatory approval of products in high-stakes domains such as drug development requires statistical evidence of safety and efficacy through large-scale randomized controlled trials. However, the high financial cost of these trials may deter developers who lack absolute certainty in their product's efficacy, ultimately stifling the development of `moonshot' products that could offer high social utility. To address this inefficiency, in this paper, we introduce a statistical protocol for experimentation where the product developer (the agent) conducts a randomized controlled trial sequentially and the regulator (the principal) partially subsidizes its cost. By modeling the protocol using a belief Markov decision process, we show that the agent's optimal strategy can be found efficiently using dynamic programming. Further, we show that the social utility is a piecewise linear and convex function over the subsidy level the principal selects, and thus the socially optimal subsidy can also be found efficiently using divide-and-conquer. Simulation experiments using publicly available data on antibiotic development and approval demonstrate that our statistical protocol can be used to increase social utility by more than $35$$\%$ relative to standard, non-sequential protocols.
author: Ander Artola Velasco, Stratis Tsirtsis, Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez

title: Safe, or Simply Incapable? Rethinking Safety Evaluation for Phone-Use Agents
content:
arXiv:2605.07630v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When a phone-use agent avoids harm, does that show safety, or simply inability to act? Existing evaluations often cannot tell. A harmful outcome may be avoided because the agent recognized the risk and chose the safe action, or because it failed to understand the screen or execute any relevant action at all. These cases have different causes and call for different fixes, yet current benchmarks often merge them under task success, refusal, or final harmful outcome. We address this problem with PhoneSafety, a benchmark of 700 safety-critical moments drawn from real phone interactions across more than 130 apps. Each instance isolates the next decision at a risky moment and asks a simple question: does the model take the safe action, take the unsafe action, or fail to do anything useful? We evaluate eight representative phone-use agents under this framework. Our results reveal two main patterns. First, stronger general phone-use ability does not reliably imply safer choices at risky moments. Models that perform better on ordinary app tasks are not always the ones that behave more safely when the next action matters. Second, failures to do anything useful behave like a capability signal rather than a safety signal: they track broader phone-use performance and increase when visual input is removed. Across models, failures split into two recurring patterns: unsafe choices in settings where the model can act but chooses wrongly, and inability to act in more visually and operationally demanding screens. Overall, a harmless outcome is not enough to count as evidence of safety. Evaluating phone-use agents requires separating unsafe judgment from inability to act. Code and public data: \url{https://github.com/tangzhy/PhoneSafety}.
author: Zhengyang Tang, Yi Zhang, Chenxin Li, Xin Lai, Pengyuan Lyu, Yiduo Guo, Weinong Wang, Junyi Li, Yang Ding, Huawen Shen, Zhengyao Fang, Xingran Zhou, Liang Wu, Fei Tang, Sunqi Fan, Shangpin Peng, Zheng Ruan, Anran Zhang, Benyou Wang, Chengquan Zhang, Han Hu

title: Large Language Models over Networks: Collaborative Intelligence under Resource Constraints
content:
arXiv:2605.08626v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming society, powering applications from smartphone assistants to autonomous driving. Yet cloud-based LLM services alone cannot serve a growing class of applications, including those operating under intermittent connectivity, sub-second latency budgets, data-residency constraints, or sustained high-volume inference. On-device deployment is in turn constrained by limited computation and memory. No single endpoint can deliver high-quality service across this spectrum. This article focuses on collaborative intelligence, a paradigm in which multiple independent LLMs distributed across device and cloud endpoints collaborate at the task level through natural language or structured messages. Such collaboration strives for superior response quality under heterogeneous resource constraints spanning computation, memory, communication, and cost across network tiers. We present collaborative inference along two complementary and composable dimensions: vertical device-cloud collaboration and horizontal multi-agent collaboration, which can be combined into hybrid topologies in practice. We then examine learning to collaborate, addressing the training of routing policies and the development of cooperative capabilities among LLMs. Finally, we identify open research challenges including scaling under resource heterogeneity and trustworthy collaborative intelligence.
author: Liangqi Yuan, Wenzhi Fang, Shiqiang Wang, H. Vincent Poor, Christopher G. Brinton

title: Nexus : An Agentic Framework for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
content:
arXiv:2605.14389v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Language models have emerged as highly capable reasoners, yet their performance in time series forecasting remains uneven across domains and levels of contextual grounding. This is primarily due to their suboptimal time series reasoning and numerical modeling capabilities. To tackle this, we introduce Nexus, a multimodal forecasting framework that bridges qualitative event reasoning with structural numerical modeling through principled statistical synthesis. Nexus follows three structured stages: (1) Temporal profiling and anchor generation, which distills the multimodal history into a timestamped causal-temporal profile and generates a forecast anchor (2) Dual contextual outlook generation, which produces decoupled macro and micro level forecast trajectories, and (3) Bayesian synthesis, which reconciles the forecasting anchor with both contextual forecast trajectories via closed-form Gaussian updating weighted by empirical error covariances. Evaluated across three diverse forecasting benchmarks constituting eight datasets spanning rich event contexts, abrupt shocks, and purely numerical series, Nexus consistently outperforms leading time-series foundation models and language model baselines, while providing interpretable causal reasoning.
author: Sarkar Snigdha Sarathi Das, Palash Goyal, Mihir Parmar, Nanyun Peng, Vishy Tirumalashetty, Chun-Liang Li, Rui Zhang, Jinsung Yoon, Tomas Pfister

title: Buffer-Parameterized Machine Learning Surrogate Models for Cross-Technology Signal Integrity Analysis and Optimization
content:
arXiv:2605.18170v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Signal integrity (SI) analysis in printed circuit board (PCB) interconnects faces increasing complexity due to diverse integrated circuit (IC) buffer technologies, varying operating conditions, and manufacturing tolerances. Existing machine learning (ML) surrogate models for the prediction of SI metrics such as the inner eye contour, eye-height (EH), eye-width (EW), and transient waveform features often rely on fixed buffer parameters, limiting the adaptability across design and technology variations. This paper introduces a buffer-parameterized ML surrogate modeling methodology capable of handling cross-technology variations without retraining by treating IC buffer characteristics, e.g., clock frequency, supply voltage, rise/fall times, jitter, and internal resistors and capacitors, as model inputs in addition to the PCB parameters. To identify the optimal surrogate architecture for this high-dimensional space, tree-based methods (RFR/GBM), kernel methods (SVR/KRR), Gaussian process regression (GPR), and neural networks are compared. The buffer-parameterized approach is validated using a complex interconnect with a total of 44 design parameters. In addition to demonstrating strong generalization, the results show that neural networks outperform other ML models on large datasets, while the anisotropic GPR excels in low-data regimes. Finally, the practical value of the ML surrogate models is demonstrated through a cross-technology design space exploration and optimization scenario, which indicates large computational speedups for eye mask compliance checking compared to simulation.
author: Julian With\"oft, Werner John, Emre Ecik, Ralf Br\"uning, J\"urgen G\"otze

title: Mutual Information Constrained Chernoff Bottleneck
content:
arXiv:2609.37994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The classical information bottleneck (IB) measures the relevance of a representation $U$ of $X$ to a target $Y$ by $I(U;Y)$, which does not directly characterize the error of downstream decisions. For a binary hypothesis $Y$ inferred from many separately encoded observations, the optimal error exponent is the Chernoff information between the two conditional distributions of $U$ given $Y$. We study the mutual information constrained Chernoff bottleneck, which seeks an encoder that maximizes this Chernoff information subject to a rate constraint $I(U;X) \leq R$. We show that its optimal value $C(R)$ increases strictly up to $R = H(V)$, where $V$ merges the symbols of $X$ with equal likelihood ratio, remains at the uncompressed exponent beyond, and, unlike the IB curve, need not be concave. We further show that $k+1$ outputs suffice to attain $C(R)$, where $k$ is the cardinality of $V$. We propose an alternating algorithm that updates the encoder via a generalized Blahut--Arimoto algorithm and the Chernoff parameter $s$ via a nonlinear equation, and prove that its iterates remain feasible, with nondecreasing and convergent Chernoff information. Comparing with the classical IB for $n$ samples, we show that, whenever the two objectives disagree, the IB encoder has the smaller equivocation $H(Y|U^{n})$ at $n = 1$, whereas the Chernoff bottleneck has the smaller error probability and equivocation for all large $n$. Numerical experiments confirm the theory, and on real topic-detection data from the 20 Newsgroups corpus, compressing each word to only $17\%$ of its entropy retains $90\%$ of the error exponent and nearly the accuracy of the uncompressed classifier.
author: Dier Tang, Guangyue Han

title: SegTrans-Diff: A Segmented Spatiotemporal Transformer With Echo-Aware Diffusion Refinement for Long-Lead Radar Echo Extrapolation
content: Accurate long-lead radar echo extrapolation is important for severe convective weather warning, but existing models suffer from echo displacement, intensity decay, and spatial blurring, weakening high-intensity echo detection and hazard-warning effectiveness. These difficulties arise because location-critical mesoscale evolution and uncertain convective-scale details require different modeling mechanisms. Deterministic models provide more reliable echo positions but tend to produce over-smoothed forecasts, whereas generative models can recover sharper structures but may introduce positional uncertainty or spurious echoes when weakly constrained by historical echo evolution. We propose SegTrans-Diff, a framework that decomposes 0–3-h extrapolation into segmented deterministic forecasting and echo-aware diffusion refinement. SegTrans predicts echo segments under segmented temporal encoding (STE), transforming asymmetric short-input long-output forecasting into segment-wise subtasks. Its SegTrans-Block combines window-wise global attention (WWGA) and frequency-wise temporal modeling (FWTM) to capture mesoscale organization and long-horizon temporal evolution. Built upon this location-aware forecast, the diffusion branch refines convective-scale details rather than generating echoes independently. The SegTrans forecast provides echo coverage, motion path, and mesoscale morphology, while encoder-derived spatiotemporal context (STC) carries historical echo-evolution information into denoising. Echo-aware gated spectral feature refinement (EG-SFR) uses forecast-derived echo and boundary gates to guide spectral feature refinement during denoising. Experiments on Shanghai radar echo dataset show that SegTrans achieves the highest pixel-wise critical success index (CSI) and Heidke skill score (HSS) among the compared models, while SegTrans-Diff improves neighborhood-based strong-echo forecast skill. Compared with DiffCast, SegTrans-Diff reduces the Fréchet inception distance (FID) by 42.8%.
author: Fangli Wu, Huantong Geng, Jinzhong Min, Zhanpeng Shi, Shaoqiang Ma

title: 3D-S2RNet: Reconstructing 3-D Radar Reflectivity Based on Himawari AHI Measurements
content: 3-D atmospheric hydrometeors measured by radars play crucial roles in hazardous weather, such as heavy rain, hail, and strong winds, but radars only cover very limited parts of the globe. This article develops a 3-D radar reflectivity reconstruction model, 3D-S2RNet, to retrieve high-resolution (1-km Horizontally and 0.5–1-km vertically) 3-D radar reflectivity with inputs from Japanese advanced Himawari imager (AHI, 16 channel) data. 3D-S2RNet integrates a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN), 2-D/3-D attention mechanisms, and a weighted composite loss strategy to retrieve the structural details of 3-D radar reflectivity, resolving the oversmoothing issue in existing methods. 3D-S2RNet significantly outperforms the baseline U-Net model across all key metrics, achieving a nearly fivefold improvement in critical success index (CSI) for retrieving intense radar reflectivity cores ( $\ge $ 45 dBZ). It accurately reconstructs diverse weather systems, including squall lines, typhoons, frontal systems, and low-latitude rain clusters. This work provides a novel capability to retrieve 3-D radar reflectivity from geostationary satellite imager observations, which has great potential to support cloud-sensitive applications, including numerical weather prediction (NWP) initialization, severe weather nowcasting, solar energy prediction, and aviation weather forecasting.
author: Yu Qin, Yubao Liu, Xuan Wang, Qinqing Xiong, Jing Duan

title: GLRF: Underwater Image Enhancement via Global and Local Visual Reconstruction Fusion
content: Underwater images frequently suffer from severe quality degradation caused by complex environmental conditions and the scattering and absorption of light during transmission, which greatly restricts their utility in subsequent analysis and applications. To tackle this challenge, this article presents an underwater image enhancement method that converges global and local visual reconstruction fusion to improve image quality and accuracy of visual tasks, called GLRF. Specifically, we first implement global color correction using the attenuated channel compensation strategy and correct local color bias using the local overlap-weighted color compensation strategy. Subsequently, we propose a structure-constrained luminance reconstruction method with smooth brightness transitions and gradient constraints for global contrast enhancement, which reduces noise caused by uneven brightness and preserves image details, while traditional histogram-based methods may introduce noise and cause irreversible detail loss when adjusting the brightness distribution. Ultimately, we exploit wavelet decomposition and reconstruction to unsharp mask the low-frequency components and adaptively threshold denoise the high-frequency components to reconstruct a high-visibility result. The comprehensive experiments on four benchmark datasets have shown that our GLRF achieves competitive or superior performance on most evaluated metrics. Additionally, the results of our GLRF enhancement are beneficial for feature matching.
author: Ling Zhou, Hengyu Li, Peixian Zhuang, Weidong Zhang

title: Enhancing Spatiotemporal InSAR Retrieval of Snow Water Equivalent Using Multichannel and MAP Estimators
content: Differential repeat-pass interferometric synthetic aperture radar (d-InSAR) is an emerging method for retrieving seasonal snow water equivalent (SWE). The technique presents several limitations and sources of uncertainty related to decorrelation and phase ambiguities. For this reason, low-frequency bands are commonly preferred as they offer greater unambiguous retrieval ranges and coherence conservation. However, they lack sensitivity to small changes in snow mass due to long wavelengths. High-frequency bands provide higher sensitivity but suffer from decorrelation and phase wrapping under heavy snow accumulation. Future SAR satellite missions may enable simultaneous acquisitions. MultiChannel (MCh) techniques leverage the combination of statistically independent measurements to reduce noise and ambiguities. This study formulates MCh techniques for retrieving changes in SWE ( $\Delta \mathrm {SWE}$ ) using d-InSAR. Three MCh configurations were evaluated: L- and S-, L- and C-, and C- and X-bands. The theoretical performance was analyzed using the Cramér–Rao lower bound (CRLB). Experimental validation employed SodSAR, a 1–10 GHz tower-based SAR system, and compared single-band and MCh retrievals of  $\Delta \mathrm {SWE}$  against in situ snow scale measurements. Additionally, semisynthetic simulations based on ALOS-2 data and a numerical snow model are provided for assessing distributed retrievals employing spatial filtering and Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimates. Results demonstrate that MCh configurations have the potential to improve retrieval accuracy, reduce noise, and resolve phase ambiguities.
author: Jorge Jorge-Ruiz, Manu Holmberg, Juha Lemmetyinen, Ioanna Merkouriadi, Anna Kontu, Jouni Pulliainen, Jaan Praks

title: AAFNet: An Asymmetric Feature Encoding and Active Energy Modulation Network for Multimodal Remote Sensing Forest Fire Detection
content: Forest fires pose severe ecological threats, yet dedicated multimodal architectures for such complex environments remain largely underexplored. Generic multimodal methods struggle to decouple heterogeneous physical properties, resist feature contamination during dynamic fusion, and preserve the fragile boundaries of microfires against deep semantic smoothing. To address these limitations, we propose an asymmetric feature encoding and active energy modulation network (AAFNet) for multimodal remote sensing forest fire detection. First, an asymmetric feature encoding is designed at the source. Within this architecture, the geometry-aware anchor (GAA) module is proposed to adaptively fit the nonrigid boundaries of smoke via decoupled deformable sampling. In parallel, the thermal-aware salient (TAS) module performs hierarchical wide-range perception operators to capture long-range thermal gradients and suppress radiation artifacts. Second, an energy-guided modulation (EGM) mechanism is formulated to dynamically allocate modality weights by quantifying instantaneous energy responses. This active regulation suppresses background interference and improves feature purity during fusion. Third, a decoupled difference reconstruction (DDR) unit is developed to explicitly reconstruct residual differences between adjacent feature hierarchies. This compensation maximizes the preservation of fine-grained textures for early stage fires. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach. The proposed model achieves an mAP@50 of 75.2%, an mAP@50–95 of 52.1% on forest fire datasets with only 2.531 M parameters, which comprehensively outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both detection accuracy and deployment parameters. Moreover, cross-dataset evaluation further demonstrates the generalization capability of AAFNet under diverse environmental distributions.
author: Qinwen Li, Haiyan Li, Fuhua Ge, Pengfei Yu, Guanbo Wang, Xiang Liu, Yitong Fu, Jinde Cao

title: Multimodal Text-to-Set Remote Sensing Image Generation With Anchor Diffusion
content: Multimodal remote sensing imagery provides complementary information for Earth observation, yet acquiring large-scale, spatially aligned multimodal data is expensive and labor-intensive, motivating data-efficient multimodal image generation. Existing methods are primarily developed for single-modal synthesis or pairwise cross-modal generation and thus cannot explicitly model the scene structure shared by multiple modalities for multimodal set generation. This limitation makes it difficult to simultaneously preserve cross-modal spatial alignment and modality-specific fidelity. To address these issues, we propose anchor diffusion (AnchorDiff), a unified framework that is able to generate spatially aligned multimodal remote sensing images from textual descriptions. To enable text-to-set generation and multimodal spatial alignment, the proposed framework produces an optical image from the given text, which is then used to construct a modality-shared scene anchor as an explicit structural prior. Specifically, we devise a UNet-based AnchorMap extractor to learn a modality-shared anchor map from modality-specific patterns to constrain structural consistency across modalities. For the multimodal generative network, we implement a conditional diffusion with a structure–attention hybrid sampling (SA-Hybrid) strategy that integrates anchor-based structural control and reference-attention guidance, thus enhancing structural alignment while maintaining modality-specific fidelity. Experiments on benchmarks covering optical, multispectral, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), and digital elevation model (DEM) data show that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of both spatial alignment and modality-specific fidelity. Code will be available at https://github.com/kyh433/Anchor-Diff
author: Yuhan Kang, Honghu Pan, Hao Liu, Qiang Liu, Weiying Xie, Leyuan Fang, Lorenzo Bruzzone

title: Bridging the Gap of Missing Modalities: Common-Specific Knowledge Learning Network for Multimodal Remote Sensing Image Classification
content: Multimodal learning has attracted significant attention in the field of remote sensing image classification due to its superior performance. Although multimodal data are often available during training, certain modalities may be unavailable during inference in real-world applications, posing a risk of performance degradation. To this end, we propose a novel common-specific knowledge learning network (CSKLNet) to bridge the gap of missing modalities. CSKLNet consists of two learning stages. First, complete multimodal knowledge is distilled from the teacher into the student under missing modalities, with the Wasserstein distance adopted to alleviate representation heterogeneity by minimizing feature distribution discrepancies. Second, two parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapters are inserted into the distilled student model to further exploit specific information from the available modalities. Compared with existing methods, CSKLNet not only inherits the common information from complete modalities but also fully leverages the available modality-specific information, thereby maintaining robust performance with missing modalities. Extensive experiments conducted on four distinct datasets indicate the advanced performance of the proposed method compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, with overall accuracy (OA) improvements of 1.34%–13.34%, 0.35%–3.54%, 0.55%–17.65%, and 0.17%–11.91% for hyperspectral image (HSI)–light detection and ranging (LiDAR) Houston2013, Trento, HSI–multispectral (MS) Houston2013, and QAI-Mangrove, respectively. The source code will be available at: https://github.com/ZhaohuiXue/CSKLNet
author: Simin Zhu, Zhaohui Xue, Hao Wu

title: 2DTS-MixNet: A Lightweight Mixing Network for Efficient Crop Classification Across Diverse Cropping Systems
content: Accurate and timely crop type classification is essential for agricultural monitoring, food security assessment, and agricultural policy making. As crop mapping is increasingly required to identify fine-grained crop types and complex cropping systems, dense satellite time series are needed to characterize subtle phenological differences and spectral variations among crop types. However, long and dense temporal observations substantially increase the computational burden, which limits the efficiency of large-scale crop classification. To address this, a lightweight mixing network, named 2-D temporal–spectral MixNet (2DTS-MixNet), is proposed for crop classification from satellite time series. Annual long time series are first transformed into a 2-D temporal–spectral (2DTS) representation, where temporal observations are arranged in a 2-D layout and spectral bands are stacked along the channel dimension. Local temporal–spectral patterns, long-range phenological dependencies, and cross-band interactions are then learned through nonoverlapping patch embedding, local/global temporal token mixing (GTTM), and spectral-channel mixing modules, respectively. The proposed method was evaluated in four typical cropping systems, including a 27-class complex crop classification scenario in the United States, a large-area crop classification scenario in France, fragmented smallholder fields in Kenya, and multiseason cropping systems in Brazil. The results showed that 2DTS-MixNet achieved the best average performance among the compared state-of-the-art methods, with an average overall accuracy (OA) of 66.89% across the four study areas. In terms of end-to-end mapping efficiency, the total time cost of the complete mapping workflow was reduced by up to approximately 37%. Overall, 2DTS-MixNet provides an efficient and scalable lightweight modeling method for crop classification from satellite time series, and can support large-scale crop mapping and rapid agricultural monitoring across diverse cropping systems.
author: Hengbin Wang, Xinyue Li, Ruixiang Huo, Yuanyuan Zhao, Shaoming Li, Xiaodong Zhang, Zhe Liu

title: The Neuro-Physical Inverter: A Modular Framework for Magnetotelluric Inversion Coupling Ensemble Conditioning With Residual Learning
content: We present the neuro-physical inverter (NPI), a modular, uncertainty-aware framework for geophysical inversion that couples ensemble-based conditioning with constrained residual learning, demonstrated in the 1-D magnetotelluric (MT) setting as a controlled testbed. The framework operates in two stages. An Ensemble-Conditional Gaussian Process (EnsCGP) conditions a prior ensemble of resistivity models on the observed response, producing a physically admissible reference ensemble. A residual-learning neural network then predicts targeted corrections to this reference, trained on synthetic data and fine-tuned per station for field application through a physics-coupled objective. Because an ensemble is conditioned, refined, and propagated through both stages, every estimate carries an associated ensemble spread. Synthetic experiments show that NPI systematically reduces ensemble-mean error without destabilizing the ensemble. Applied to broadband MT data from the Gabbs Valley geothermal region (Nevada, USA), NPI reduces the across-station mean misfit over the mid-period band while retaining comparable ensemble spread. The propagated ensemble yields a factor of uncertainty that serves as an operational measure of constraint within the assumed model class. Both stages are dimension-agnostic in formulation, and the design principles established here are intended to scale to higher-dimensional parameterizations.
author: Jae Deok Kim, Sai Ravela, Rob. L. Evans

title: Radar-Referenced Prior Network for Infrared Iceberg Detection
content: In polar waters, ice floes and icebergs pose a threat to navigation safety. Detecting these hazards with shipborne infrared cameras has attracted attention and is being developed. The single sensor is limited in performance under the requirements of extreme cold, fog, and long-range detection, which greatly limits its ability to meet the actual requirements for navigation safety. Introducing spatial position information from navigation radars can assist infrared sensors in achieving precise detection of sea ice targets. In this article, we propose a radar-referenced prior network (RRPNet) and construct an infrared-radar multimodal iceberg target (IRMIT) dataset. For the heterogeneity of infrared and radar data, a dual-source feature extraction (DSFE) encoder is designed to extract the semantic features of infrared and the prior information of radar positions. Then, we propose the detection-reference alignment module (DRAM), which utilizes the cross-modal spatial correlation mechanism to guide the mapping of the position of the radar to the semantic space of infrared. Finally, the multistage feature fusion (MFF) module is designed to enhance the representation ability of ice target features and suppress redundant information across modalities. The experimental results on the IRMIT dataset show that the proposed method effectively improves the performance of infrared ice detection and can achieve effective and robust detection in extremely complex scenarios.
author: Xinyu Ma, Yang Li, Fanglin Chen, Fuhai Guo, Fulin Su

title: ER-Net: Evolutionary Refinement Architecture With Spectral Purification for Infrared Small Target Detection
content: Infrared small target detection (ISTD) remains challenging because extremely weak target signals are often submerged in strong, nonstationary background clutter. Although deep-learning methods have advanced considerably, many architectures exhibit approximately isotropic low-pass behavior, causing irreversible attenuation of the high-frequency details of dim targets in deep layers. This article proposes an evolutionary refinement network (ER-Net), a detection framework that mitigates information dissipation through recursive feature refinement. Its central contribution is an asymmetric enhancement path: instead of using a conventional symmetric architecture, ER-Net treats the raw infrared (IR) image as an independent reference stream that bypasses shallow sampling and enters the deep hub directly, thereby supplying prior guidance at the most information-sensitive levels. First, a spectral purification module (SPM) performs adaptive feature cleaning in the frequency domain to suppress background noise while enhancing target-salient responses. Second, an evolutionary refinement hub (ER-Hub) uses global statistical fingerprints of the raw image to control feature evolution dynamically. The hub combines an Evolutionary Refinement Unit (ERU), which progressively strengthens and concentrates weak-target responses through recursive refinement, with residual synergistic fusion (RSF), which corrects residual errors and compensates for signal loss in nonlinear mappings. Extensive experiments on Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics (NUAA)-single-frame infrared small target (SIRST), National University of Defense Technology (NUDT)-SIRST, and infrared small target detection (IRSTD)-1K show that ER-Net achieves a competitive overall balance in pixel-level localization and background suppression. With a lightweight parameter count and high desktop inference efficiency, ER-Net provides an architecture–performance trade-off suitable for efficient IR detection in complex scenes. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/LXJK123/ER-Net.git
author: Sheng-Yu Dai, Jian-Hua Qin, Zhong Liu, Hong-Wang Zhao, Xue-Qin Zhao, Ting-Ting Huang

title: Retrieving Specific Differential Phase for Dual-Frequency Dual-Polarization Doppler Cloud Radar
content: The specific differential phase ( $K_{\text {DP}}$ ) is an indispensable polarimetric radar variable for investigating the microphysical properties of precipitation. Utilizing the differential propagation phase ( $\Phi _{\text {DP}}$ ) identified by a Rayleigh plateau detection algorithm based on the differential reflectivity ( $Z_{\text {DR}}$ ) spectra, the reflectivity differential phase (ZPHI) approach is extended to retrieve  $K_{\text {DP}}$  for a frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) dual-frequency (one is at 35 GHz and the other is at 95 GHz) dual-polarization Doppler cloud radar. Three constraints are imposed on the ZPHI approach, including a range-partitioning scheme based on the fluctuation characteristics of  $\Phi _{\text {DP}}$ , a nonnegative constraint on the specific attenuation, and a convergence constraint to terminate the calculation. The  $Z_{\text {DR}}$  and  $\Phi _{\text {DP}}$  spectra during a stratiform precipitation event on February 3, 2021, and the raindrop size and distribution drop size and distribution (DSD) dataset collected by a disdrometer deployed in Cabauw, The Netherlands, are utilized to demonstrate its practical performance. The result shows that: 1) the ZPHI approach is effectively extended to retrieve  $K_{\text {DP}}$  in dominant Mie scattering situations. Radar-retrieved  $K_{\text {DP}}$  at both frequencies can be well derived with a high spatio-temporal resolution, and agree well with DSD-derived  $K_{\text {DP}}$  across the precipitation event; 2) the combined use of  $\delta _{\text {co}}$ ,  $V_{\text {R}}$ , and  $K_{\text {DP}}$  can adequately describe the relevant microphysical characteristics for the stratiform precipitation event, which agrees well with the evolution of surface DSD-derived  $D_{0}$ ; and 3) the impacts of short-duration DSD changes can be well captured by the fluctuated  $K_{\text {DP}}$  and  $\delta _{\text {co}}$  at both frequencies, and the drop shape ratio (DSR) changes explain the residual  $K_{\text {DP}}$  deviations at Ka-band, as another potential response to DSD changes within radar range bins.
author: Yabin Gou, Christine Unal, Herman Russchenburg

title: Wideband RFI Mitigation for Spaceborne SAR by Acquiring Prior Information via Time–Frequency Analysis
content: Operating in shared frequency bands, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) faces a complex electromagnetic environment, making radio frequency interference (RFI), particularly wideband interference (WBI), an increasingly prominent issue. WBI typically exhibits time-varying characteristics across pulses, with its amplitude and temporal location varying significantly. Despite these variations, WBI originating from the same source generally maintains stable intrinsic properties, such as bandwidth and duration, which can serve as useful prior information for WBI mitigation. However, due to the difficulty of WBI modeling, existing mitigation methods often bypass WBI parameter extraction, neglecting the utilization of prior information. Furthermore, these methods typically apply fixed filtering strategies across the entire WBI-containing pulse, ignoring variations in scattering intensity across different terrains. This leads to degraded mitigation performance in complex scenes. To address these issues, a WBI mitigation method that acquires prior information is proposed in this article. Specifically, through time–frequency analysis, WBI prior information is extracted from representative pulses identified via a spectral flatness indicator. WBI localization can be achieved by independently clustering strong- and weak-scattering regions, further optimized by the prior information. Finally, the eigen-subspace projection (ESP) method is applied to the localized time–frequency regions to mitigate WBI. Comprehensive experimental results on SAR data from diverse scenes confirm the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.
author: Zijun Li, Zongsen Lv, Yanyang Liu, Ning Li, Lei Cui

title: DHMD: Harnessing the Power of State-Space Models for Advanced Vehicle-Aware RGB–T Object Detection in Spatial–Frequency Domain
content: Red-green-blue–thermal (RGB–T) multimodal object detection has become an effective paradigm for robust remote sensing perception by exploiting the complementary characteristics of visible (VI) and thermal imagery. However, existing convolutional neural network (CNN)- and Transformer-based RGB–T detectors still suffer from several limitations, including insufficient global context modeling or high computational cost, modality heterogeneity and cross-modal feature misalignment, inadequate spatial–frequency feature interaction, and weak perception of small vehicles in complex remote sensing scenes. To address these challenges, this article proposes a novel dual-head Mamba detector (DHMD), an accuracy-oriented RGB–T detector that achieves a favorable tradeoff between detection accuracy and computational efficiency for remote sensing vehicle detection. The proposed method focuses on two fundamental aspects: cross-modal discrepancy modeling and task-aware vehicle representation. First, to address the semantic misalignment and spatial–frequency representation discrepancy between RGB and thermal modalities, DHMD establishes a unified cross-modal representation learning strategy. A dual-Mamba backbone is employed to efficiently capture long-range dependencies with linear computational complexity, while an align-fuse module for semantic flow (AFMSF) alleviates cross-modal semantic misalignment through bimodal semantic enhancement, learnable semantic flow field prediction, and deformable alignment-based feature fusion. Meanwhile, a space–frequency interactive mixer (SFIM) jointly models spatial structures and frequency-domain information to strengthen spatial–frequency feature coupling and enhance the representation of small vehicles. Second, to address the small-scale, densely distributed, and geometrically structured characteristics of remote sensing vehicles, a task-aware vehicle representation strategy is developed by incorporating vehicle-aware geometric priors into adaptive multiscale feature fusion through a rectangular self-adaptive calibration adaptive spatial feature fusion (RSC-ASFF) module, thereby improving the robustness of vehicle perception in complex scenes. Extensive experiments on the DroneVehicle, vehicle detection in aerial imagery (VEDAI), and M3FD datasets demonstrate that DHMD achieves state-of-the-art detection performance, obtaining mAP50 scores of 0.834, 0.679, and 0.848, respectively. These results validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework for red-green-blue–thermal (RGB–T) remote sensing vehicle detection.
author: Chengrui Yu, Guangxin Li, Baolin Lv, Yuanhao Gong, Yao Fu, Yuyang Huang, Chang Yu, Xiaonan Jiang

title: SDMCNet: Spatial–Spectral Decoupled Mamba–MoE Collaborative Network for Hyperspectral Image Classification
content: Using the whole image as input for hyperspectral image (HSI) classification, the model needs to handle broader spatial dependencies and more diverse spectral variations. In modeling nonlocal spatial relationships, scanning based on fixed windows is prone to directional bias, leading to the loss of spatial boundary details. In addition, the high dimensionality of the data makes spectral distributions complex and spectral information redundant, thereby affecting the reliable identification and effective utilization of spectral bands. To address these challenges, we propose SDMCNet, a spatial–spectral decoupled Mamba–mixture-of-expert (MoE) collaborative network for image-level HSI classification. Taking the whole image as input, SDMCNet achieves a balance between spatial structure modeling and fine-grained spectral representation. Specifically, the spatial branch progressive spatial perception feature extraction (PSPFE) integrates local and global Mamba modules to capture short- and long-range spatial contextual dependencies. A boundary constrained enhancement module (BCEM) is further introduced to suppress oversmoothing and noisy perturbations near class boundaries, thereby preserving spatial boundary details. The spectral branch anchor routed expert spectral aggregation (ARESA) builds an anchor routed expert collaboration mechanism to adaptively select complementary spectral experts to model complex dependencies among spectral bands and obtain precise spectral band combinations. The two branches collaborate through spectral channel weighting, thereby achieving synergistic spatial–spectral modeling for image-level HSI classification. Extensive experiments on the Indian Pines (IP), Pavia University (PU), Houston 2013, and HanChuan (HC) datasets demonstrate that SDMCNet consistently outperforms representative methods, validating the effectiveness and potential value of using the whole image as input for HSI classification. The code is available at https://github.com/chai-xue/SDMCNet
author: Xue Chai, Bingbing Lei, Wei Feng, Ruiqing Zhang, Zhipeng Liu

title: Adaptive Calibration for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning Hyperspectral Image Classification
content: Coastal wetland hyperspectral image classification (HSIC) is practically constrained by scarce labeled samples. Cross-domain few-shot learning (CDFSL) provides a promising solution by enabling knowledge transfer under limited supervision. However, coastal wetlands exhibit high spectral similarity and spatial heterogeneity. Existing CDFSL methods struggle to disentangle such complex geomorphology, leading to insufficient feature discriminability. Furthermore, severe prototype estimation bias and domain shift persist as inherent challenges. To address these issues, an adaptive calibration strategy for CDFSL is proposed. Specifically, a collaborative perception feature extractor (CPFE) with a spectral–spatial adaptive differencing module (SSAD) and a dual-stream gated fusion module (DGFM) is constructed to extract the fine-grained signatures and complex spatial structures. Building upon these robust representations, we design a dynamic prototype interaction calibration (DPIC) module, which adaptively distinguishes typical samples from hard samples via the prediction confidence of query samples, thereby constructing and fusing multiple auxiliary prototypes to enable class prototypes to better approximate the latent data distribution. Finally, we develop a synergistic global domain alignment (SGDA) strategy that jointly aligns macroscopic spatial distributions and spectral baselines while preserving class-discriminative structures. Extensive experiments on three self-constructed hyperspectral image (HSI) datasets and one public dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed CDFSL method for HSIC via adaptive calibration (ACFSL).
author: Zhongwei Li, Wenhui Peng, Qixing Yu, Fangming Guo, Guangbo Ren, Jianbu Wang, Xinchen Lu

title: HMMamba: A Heterogeneous Multibranch Mamba Architecture for Hyperspectral Image Classification
content: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification is crucial for applications like precision agriculture and urban planning, necessitating the effective integration of spatial and spectral features. However, existing methods often struggle with limited receptive fields, structural damage from data transformation, or high computational complexity, hindering an optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we propose HMMamba—a lightweight, accurate, and interpretable heterogeneous multibranch architecture (HMBA). Its core innovation lies in our first proposal of the structured Mamba modeler (SMM), which sequences and reconstructs high-dimensional data through structure-preserving axial compaction and recombination, employing an orientation-separated shared Mamba mechanism to efficiently achieve global dependency modeling. The framework is further augmented by a lightweight anisotropy perceiver (AP) for mid-range spatial structures and a detail enhancer (DE) for local discriminative features. These three complementary branches collectively construct a comprehensive multiscale feature hierarchy. Extensive experiments on five public HSI datasets demonstrate that our method achieves a top overall accuracy (OA) of 98.26%, with merely 0.44 M parameters and an inference speed of 0.01 s, significantly outperforming current convolutional neural network (CNN)-, Transformer-, and Mamba-based models. Experimental results and visualization analyses show that HMMamba excels in structural integrity, classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and interpretability, positioning it as a promising next-generation HSI classifier. The code for this work will be available at https://github.com/IIPGroup-C/HMMamba
author: Yongchao Sun, Jing Wang, Tongzhen Si, Tao Xu, Guangqi Li, Xiaohui Yang

title: From Pseudoclasses to Real Changes: Spatial–Spectral Difference Learning for Mitigating Spectral Pseudochange in Hyperspectral Change Detection
content: A core challenge in hyperspectral change detection (HCD) is spectral pseudochange, artifacts from imaging conditions that cause severe overlap between changed and unchanged samples, reducing their separability and hindering accurate detection. Existing methods, including traditional difference-driven pipelines and deep learning models, remain vulnerable to such discrepancies. To address this issue, we use pseudoclass separability as a design perspective to guide spatial–spectral representation enhancement, where changed and unchanged labels are regarded as discriminative surrogate categories defined on bitemporal spectral pairs rather than semantic land-cover categories. We propose spatial–spectral difference learning (SSDL), a spatial–spectral difference enhancement framework whose central component is spectral attention (SpeA) for peak-valley spectral-structure enhancement. SpeA is complemented by spatial differential attention (SDA) for competitive suppression of nonchange responses and position-aware multihead spectral linear self-attention (SpeLA) for spectral correlation modeling with a favorable accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Experimental results on three public HCD datasets demonstrate competitive and consistent performance, particularly in scenarios where spectral pseudochange causes strong changed/unchanged distribution overlap, and the code is available at https://github.com/WUTCM-Lab/SSDL
author: Bo Zhang, Guirong Feng, Yaxiong Chen, Bingyi Liu, Shili Xiong, Xiaoqiang Lu

title: Rethinking Multilabel Remote Sensing Image Classification Under Dual-Distribution Instance-Dependent Noise
content: Multilabel scene classification (MLC) is a fundamental task in remote sensing (RS). However, its performance is often limited by noisy annotations, where subtractive noise occurs when inconspicuous targets are missed and additive noise arises when visually confusing categories are falsely added. To simulate such annotation errors, the recently proposed instance-dependent multilabel noise (IDMN) method introduces the first instance-dependent noise generation strategy for RS MLC, driven by the intuition that hard label instances are more susceptible to mislabeling. Specifically, it leverages a single probability distribution of present labels to derive thresholds for both subtractive and additive noise generation. This design determines additive noise by requiring absent-label occurrence probabilities to exceed an irrelevant present-label threshold, leaving its quantity difficult to control and overlooking potentially confusing absent labels. To address this limitation, we propose dual-distribution IDMN (DD-IDMN), which explicitly decouples the score distributions of present and absent labels for calibrated noise generation. Empirical analysis under DD-IDMN reveals that additive noise yields more severe performance degradation than subtractive noise. To combat this DD-IDMN challenge, we propose the prompt-guided activation interference rectification network (PAIR-Net). Through cross-modal attention with learnable text prompts, it learns more discriminative RS feature representations. Furthermore, we introduce an activation-aware dynamic filtering (ADF) module to identify unreliable present labels for suppressing the more destructive additive noise under DD-IDMN. Experiments on UCMerced, AID, and MLRSNet demonstrate that PAIR-Net consistently outperforms representative noise-robust multilabel methods under complex instance-dependent noise. Our code is available at https://github.com/BasilLeave/PAIR-Net
author: Xinlei Zhang, Fan Liu, Chuanyi Zhang, Xiaoying Ji, Wenhui Wang, Wei Zhou, Jun Zhou

title: A Novel Image Change Detection Approach Based on Siamese Superpixel-Guided Graph Transformer
content: Change detection (CD) of very-high-resolution (HR) remote sensing (RS) images remains a challenging task due to complex spatial patterns and massive scale variations of land covers. Recently, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Transformers have achieved remarkable progress in this field. However, since existing Transformers and graph-fused methods generally construct nodes on regular grids or pixels, which breaks the inherent structural consistency of objects and blurs fine boundaries, they still struggle to achieve an optimal balance between capturing long-range global contexts and preserving fine-grained local geometric details (e.g., sharp boundaries) under acceptable computational costs. To address these dilemmas, a novel Siamese superpixel-guided graph convolutional Transformer (SiamSGCT) for efficient and accurate CD is proposed in this article. Specifically, a superpixel-guided graph representation (SGR) module is investigated to project dense pixel-level features into a compact graph space, inherently maintaining the structural consistency of objects. Subsequently, a graph convolutional Transformer (GCT) is utilized to model coarse-to-fine object-level semantic dependencies within the graph domain. Furthermore, to bridge the semantic gap between different topological spaces, a cross-space pixel-graph fusion (CPGF) module is proposed to deeply inject the aggregated global graph contexts back into the dense pixel domain, achieving reciprocal enhancement. Finally, to mitigate the inevitable boundary aliasing effect during graph-to-pixel reprojection, a Laplacian boundary-aware optimization strategy is introduced, which explicitly forces the network to focus on high-frequency structural information for precise contour delineation. Experiments on three widely used benchmark datasets (LEVIR-CD, WHU-CD, and CLCD) demonstrate that the proposed SiamSGCT outperforms several state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, achieving a superior tradeoff between detection accuracy and model complexity. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/maren/SiamSGCT
author: Xiaochen Lu, Diman Xiao, Shenglan Wang, Jingjing Zhang, Yajun Li

title: An Entropy-Driven Optimization Framework for Sustainable Remote Sensing Onboard Processing in Energy-Constrained LEO Networks
content: High-resolution remote sensing (HRS) missions generate large onboard imagery streams that must be transformed into timely HRS products or alerts. Direct downlink of raw RS data or fully local onboard processing is difficult for energy-constrained low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites because sensing, intersatellite transmission, computation, and downlink operations jointly stress battery depth of discharge (DoD) and thermal safety. In this article, we formulate a communication–sensing–computation coordination problem for sustainable onboard HRS processing in energy-constrained LEO networks. To solve it efficiently, we propose an entropy-based edge computing (EEC) framework that decomposes the problem into two stages: entropy-driven multiedge-LEO selection and sequential closed-form resource allocation. To support timely onboard HRS product generation, we propose a multiedge offloading model in which the sensing LEO uses its four laser intersatellite link (LISL) terminals to simultaneously offload up to four RS processing task instances to distinct edge satellites selected by the entropy-driven scoring stage. The second stage determines the minimum feasible adjustable LISL power required to sustain stable high-rate permanent-LISL offloading and then derives closed-form updates for sensing and computing frequencies while respecting energy, thermal, and delay limits. Simulations under a disaster-monitoring HRS processing workload demonstrate that EEC enables timely onboard HRS product generation by maintaining low mission-deadline violations, limiting the sensing-LEO DoD to about 21%, preserving thermal safety, and improving timely HRS product-generation reliability to about 94.2% compared with the considered baselines.
author: Ahmad Y. Alhusenat, Lei Lei, Qizhou Wang, Hana Rababah, Xingjun Zhang, Xiangyong Cao, Symeon Chatzinotas

title: First Demonstration of an Onboard Polarimetric Calibration and Ice-Cloud-Based Validation Framework for the Particulate Observing Scanning Polarimeter (POSP)
content: Accurate global measurements of atmospheric aerosols and clouds require satellite polarimetric sensors to maintain stable radiometric and polarimetric performance throughout their on-orbit operations. However, monitoring and correcting on-orbit degradation remains a challenge, as most current polarimetric sensors lack active onboard polarimetric calibration capabilities and rely heavily on vicarious calibration methods constrained by atmospheric uncertainties. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the Particulate Observing Scanning Polarimeter (POSP) onboard the GaoFen-5(02) [GF-5(02)] and DaQi-1 (DQ-1) satellites, which features a unique onboard polarimetric calibration system. Analyzing data from the first one to two years of operation, we identified significant temporal drifts in the calibration coefficients for the short-wave infrared (SWIR) bands (1610 and 2250 nm). These SWIR drifts are consistent with the high thermal sensitivity of the detectors in the on-orbit environment. In addition, the calibration coefficients of the two independent instruments exhibit coherent periodic fluctuations across multiple bands, suggesting the influence of common external thermal and radiative conditions. To independently validate the onboard calibration updates, high-altitude ice clouds observed at scattering angles larger than 170° were used as approximately unpolarized natural References. The validation results demonstrate that the dynamically updated onboard calibration coefficients substantially improve the SWIR polarimetric accuracy. After calibration, the median degree of linear polarization (DoLP) residuals of the SWIR bands agree with the simulated intrinsic ice-cloud DoLP to within one standard deviation of the simulated ensemble. The daily DoLP time series further confirm that the upward drift in the SWIR bands is effectively removed after calibration. Moreover, the validation results reveal a clear latitude dependence: mid-to-high-latitude ice clouds provide more stable and lower uncertainty references than low-latitude ice clouds, which exhibit noticeable seasonal DoLP increases. Overall, this study provides the first on-orbit evaluation of an active onboard polarimetric calibration system, quantifies SWIR-band calibration drifts and cross-platform periodic variations, validates the onboard updates with large scattering angle ice clouds, and establishes a transferable calibration and validation (Cal/Val) framework for future spaceborne polarimetric missions.
author: Xuefeng Lei, Zhenhai Liu, Cheng Chen, Gaojun Chi, Haixiao Yu, Zhihui Wang, Congfei Li, Zhenyang Li, Haofei Wang, Yuyang Chang, Guangfeng Xiang, Binghuan Meng, Zhen Liu, Christian Matar, Chong Li, Maoxin Song, Zhenwei Qiu, Zhengqiang Li, Oleg Dubovik, Jin Hong

title: LAGF-FracNet: Liquid ODE-Driven Adaptive Graph Fusion for Fine-Grained Geological Body Segmentation in Borehole Electrical Images
content: In borehole-scale geophysical remote sensing, electrical imaging logging actively acquires subsurface electrical responses and provides millimeter-scale borehole wall texture information for identifying geological bodies such as fractures and bedding. However, accurate pixel-wise segmentation of such borehole imaging data remains challenging. The difficulty arises from the elongated morphology, weak boundaries, sparse spatial distribution of fracture- and bedding-related targets, as well as pseudo-responses induced by complex borehole conditions and cross-well distribution shifts. To address these issues, this study proposes, namely the liquid ODE-driven adaptive graph fusion fracture network (LAGF-FracNet), a dual-branch deep learning framework for geological body segmentation in borehole electrical imaging logs. The framework integrates a convolutional neural network and a Swin Transformer (Swin-T) to jointly model local textural details and global structural semantics. Furthermore, continuous feature evolution, cross-branch alignment, adaptive graph fusion, and tri-decoder joint supervision are introduced to enhance structural representation, heterogeneous feature interaction, and decoding consistency. The proposed framework is designed for intelligent interpretation of borehole-scale remote sensing images under complex subsurface imaging conditions, aiming to improve the automated segmentation and characterization of fractures and bedding-related structures for logging interpretation and reservoir evaluation. The method was validated on two datasets, namely EIL-I and EIL-II. EIL-I is an in-house dataset constructed from 21 wells in the Sichuan Basin, whereas EIL-II is a public dataset derived from the Utah FORGE project. On EIL-I, LAGF-FracNet achieves 98.24% precision, 89.76% recall, 93.81%  $F1$ -score, 86.98% mean intersection over union (mIoU), and 97.76% mean pixel accuracy (mPA). On EIL-II, it obtains 91.63% precision, 89.25% recall, 90.42%  $F1$ -score, 85.16% mIoU, and 93.61% mPA. Experimental results demonstrate that LAGF-FracNet effectively preserves structural continuity, suppresses pseudo-responses, and maintains consistent performance across the two evaluated datasets, indicating its potential for borehole-scale remote sensing interpretation and reservoir evaluation.
author: Huazhong Yang, Zhiliang Zhang, Jiahui Zhang, Liu Jun, Chong Zhang

title: Physics-Informed Blind Deconvolution for Seismic Resolution Enhancement Based on Zero-Shot Learning
content: The limited seismic resolution significantly degrades thin beds identification and reservoir characterization. Conventional deconvolution methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, while supervised deep learning (DL) methods require extensive high-fidelity labels. Although some unsupervised methods reduce the dependence on labels, they often lack geophysical interpretability. In addition, most DL-based deconvolution methods assume a known wavelet, which limits their applicability in practical scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a physics-informed blind deconvolution workflow for seismic resolution enhancement based on zero-shot learning. Specifically, a three-stage progressive optimization strategy is proposed. An initial wavelet is first estimated by amplitude spectrum constraints and phase scanning. A dual-stream time–frequency network (DSTFNet) is then warmed up with the wavelet fixed to obtain a reliable initial reflectivity. Finally, the wavelet and the network parameters are alternately updated to achieve joint refinement of the wavelet and the reflectivity. In addition, we construct a joint loss function consisting of a physics-constrained Huber loss, and an L1 sparsity loss, which enhances physical interpretability and robustness to noise. Experiments on synthetic and field data demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits strong generalization and robustness.
author: Wenshuo Yu, Shiqi Dong, Hongyuan Yang, Xintong Dong

title: Robust Marine CSEM Signal Enhancement in Low-SNR Environments Using a Mixed Multistable Stochastic Pooling Network
content: The marine controlled-source electromagnetic (MCSEM) method is used to reconstruct deep subsurface resistivity distributions. However, low-frequency ambient noise and instrumental interference reduce the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of observed responses and degrade the stability of resistivity inversion. To address this noise-induced inversion degradation under low-SNR conditions, this study proposes a signal enhancement framework that integrates a mixed multistable stochastic resonance (MMSR) model with an adaptive stochastic pooling network (SPN). The MMSR model enhances the target-frequency components of MCSEM responses while suppressing uncorrelated noise. Parallel stochastic resonance (SR) nodes are constructed for multichannel signal fusion, allowing the framework to accommodate complex noise patterns. A recursive least squares (RLSs) algorithm is then used to adaptively optimize the pooling weights for further signal enhancement. Synthetic results show that the multistable SR–stochastic pooling network (MMSR-SPN) method improves the average SNR by 13.79 dB and maintains consistent enhancement performance under varying noise levels. Field datasets further validate its practical applicability. The processed time-series waveforms exhibit more pronounced attenuation and periodic features, attaining a spectrum improvement ratio (SIR) of 14.2. The magnitude-versus-offset (MVO) and phase-versus-offset (PVO) curves become smoother and more continuous, and the derived inversion results are consistent with known stratigraphic records. Numerical simulations and field-data experiments confirm that the proposed framework effectively alleviates noise-induced inversion instability, providing a robust signal enhancement solution for geophysical electromagnetic exploration.
author: Yihan Tian, Wanyue Zhang, Fan Yang, Suyi Li

title: Natural Fracture Identification From Conventional Well Logs Using Geology-Aware Relative Anomaly Representation and Anchor-Constrained Interval Decoding
content: Reliable identification of natural fractures from conventional well logs is complicated by nonunique fracture signatures under lithofacies heterogeneity and interwell baseline drift. Pointwise classifiers tend to fragment fracture zones, whereas unconstrained sequence models may overextend them. Depth-wise autocorrelation further complicates performance evaluation by producing overly optimistic estimates. We propose geology-aware interval decoding (GAID) to address these limitations through two methodological advances and a leakage-aware evaluation design. First, a geology-background-conditioned representation expresses fracture-sensitive responses as local deviations while incorporating multilog consistency and stratigraphic context, thereby improving response comparability across wells. Second, candidate-anchor-constrained decoding separates pointwise candidate localization from contextual assessment and permits interval expansion only within finite neighborhoods of candidate anchors, limiting boundary drift and error propagation. Evaluation combines leave-one-well-out (LOWO) testing, an independently held-out well, spatial-separation audits, and strict, depth-tolerant, and event-level metrics. Under threefold LOWO validation, GAID achieved well-averaged strict and ±0.25-m-tolerant  $F1$  scores of 75.60% and 85.39%, respectively. These exceeded the strongest deep-learning baseline by 3.57 and 3.32 percentage points, respectively. Random pointwise splitting yielded a strict  $F1$  score 12.45 percentage points higher than LOWO validation, highlighting the sensitivity of performance estimates to the validation protocol. GAID achieved a ±0.25-m-tolerant  $F1$  score of 88.12% on a predesignated held-out shale well. On a held-out tight-sandstone well, it achieved a strict  $F1$  score of 75.27% after target-domain retraining. These results support GAID as a structured and leakage-aware workflow for cross-well fracture identification, without implying zero-shot cross-lithology transfer.
author: Shiqiang Liu, Lianbo Zeng, Jiarui Zhang, Xiaoyu Du, Baoyu Liang, Zhen Wang
